parts: Clothes get dirty with dirt, grease and perspiration and lose strength and appearance, so they must be cared for. Laundering means washing, drying and finishing of clothes; dry cleaning cleans without water using solvents and grease absorbents. Steps in laundering: mending (tears, loose buttons), stain removal (before washing, or stains spread and fix), sorting (by fibre type: cotton, wool, silk, synthetics; whites separate from coloured; very dirty separate), soaking (loosens dirt; not for non-fast colours and not for woollens, which felt), washing, rinsing (2–4 times until all soap is removed), starching and bluing, drying (whites in sun, coloured in shade, silk in shade, synthetics on a hanger in shade, woollens flat in shade) and ironing and pressing (cotton damp with a hot iron, silk damp, synthetics and rayon moderately hot, woollens over damp muslin).

A detergent is a cleansing product: a soap (from natural oil, fat and waxes) or a syndet (synthetic, from chemicals). Both lower the surface tension of water. Syndets wet the fabric more readily, dissolve in hot and cold water, work in hard water (soaps foam well only in soft water), smell sweet, already have blues and optical brightening agents, leave no deposits (soap leaves soapy deposits that make clothes dull) and are more economical in the long run, though soaps are cheaper. Auxiliaries are products other than cleansers that give a good finish: blues, optical brightening agents, chemical bleaches, stain-removing agents and stiffening agents (starch gives a crisp finish). Blue counteracts yellowness of white cottons and linens; apply just before the last rinse after mixing thoroughly (ultramarine and Prussian blue). Optical brightening agents (OBA or FBA) are colourless fluorescent dyes that absorb ultraviolet light and reflect visible light, making clothes whiter; no chemical action. Chemical bleaches whiten by oxidising or reducing action. Oxidising bleaches (almost permanent; for cotton and linen): sunlight (the oldest, simplest; wet the stain and put it on grass), Javelle water (sodium hypochlorite; dilute and rinse well), potassium permanganate with oxalic acid (brown stains such as rust, paan, dyes, mildew, perspiration and ink) and hydrogen peroxide (universal bleach for animal and vegetable fibres; store in dark bottles). Reducing bleaches (milder; for wool and silk, which may turn yellow again): sodium hydrosulphite and sodium bisulphite.

A stain is a mark other than dirt. Identify by colour, smell and feel (curry and pickle yellow; tea and coffee brown; grass green; paint and sugar syrup stiff; lipstick and shoe polish slippery). Categories: vegetable (curry, tea, coffee), animal (milk, blood), grease (butter, shoe polish), mineral (rust), grass and miscellaneous (dyes). Methods: dipping, sponging, drop method and steaming. Precautions: treat stains fresh, know the fabric, identify the stain, start with simple methods and wash with cold water first for protein stains like blood and egg (hot water coagulates them), test chemicals on a small portion, repeated mild reagents are better than one strong one, wash with soapy solution at the end and dry in the sun. Examples: fresh tea or coffee on white cotton: pour boiling water; old: glycerine and sodium perborate or hydrogen peroxide; coloured cotton: soak in warm water with borax; fresh blood: wash with cold water and soap; old blood: salt water (2 tablespoons in half a bucket); fresh curry or butter: hot water and soap or talcum powder; paint, shoe polish, nail polish, lipstick and ball pen: rub with spirit or kerosene; grass: soap and water, old: methylated spirit; paan: paste of onion; mehndi: warm milk; rust: lime juice and salt.

Choice depends on how dirty and what fabric. Friction washing (strong cottons: by hand, with a plastic brush for very soiled things like dusters, or beating with a stick for large articles); suction washing (heavy pile fabrics such as towels, with a suction washer creating a vacuum); kneading and squeezing (delicate silks, woollens and rayon; gentle, no change of shape); machine washing. Wool: no soaking, lukewarm water, light pressure, liquid soap or reetha solution (not for whites), dry flat. Silk: no soaking, lukewarm water. Synthetics: lukewarm or cold water, no hot water as they melt. Storage: empty pockets and brush, sun and air worn clothes, do not let them get too dirty, never store damp clothes (mildew), and protect from insects with tobacco, dried neem, camphor and moth balls; woollens packed in newspaper because moths dislike printer's ink.
